source.version_note: Published 4 May 2023, Motivation and Emotion 47:781–794. The abstract's moral-acceptability direction conflicts with Tables 2–3 and the main results/discussion.

citation.title: Framing self-sacrifice in the investigation of moral judgment and moral emotions in human and autonomous driving dilemmas

reading.source_scope_note: Human first-person hypothetical choices and immediate moral/emotion ratings across human-driving and autonomous-passenger scenarios. Fixed textual dilemmas; no deployed AI, real injury, objective moral correctness or machine affect tested.
access_limits: All 14 extracted pages read, including theory, scenario examples, procedure, models, numeric tables, discussion, limitations and references. Page 8 tables and contrary main-results wording also visually inspected.
Full 12 scenario texts, raw data, code and detailed model-selection output on the external OSF were not independently opened or rerun. Cited emotion primary works/books remain unread.

study.design: Within-person 2x2: active manual driver versus passive full-automation passenger; own sacrifice in utilitarian versus non-utilitarian option; three different scenarios per cell
study.language: Italian; examples translated to English in article
study.procedure: Random scenario order; alternative order randomized; second option after 7 seconds, decision after another 7; both alternatives then rated for acceptability, followed by present shame/guilt/anger/disgust
study.scales: Acceptability and emotions 0–7; hypothetical binary choice
study.analysis: Binomial mixed model for choice and six linear mixed models; participant random intercepts, forward stepwise/Akaike-weight selection; no stated scenario random effects

summary: No new independent construct. Add direct human self-report evidence to shame, guilt, moral anger and moral disgust. The primary source clarifies a misleading secondary lead: self-sacrificial utilitarian options are chosen less often but rated MORE morally acceptable in its tables/main text, contrary to the abstract's less-moral wording. Retain that contradiction and update the earlier Dong review's source trail.

findings.term: Self-evaluation after a hypothetical choice differs from a general negative moral verdict
findings.definition: After a hypothetical choice, participants rate their own present shame, with reported intensities depending on personal involvement and whether the preferred option protects or sacrifices themselves.
findings.novelty_rationale: A second fully read paper offers a direct human measure relevant to the existing shame entry; no duplicate ID or new affective mechanism is introduced.

This is human self-report, not an internal model state. The abstract/main-text moral-acceptability direction conflicts and sample percentages need reconciliation.

findings.term: Self-referred guilt is measured after the respondent's own hypothetical choice
findings.definition: Participants report present guilt after choosing between fictional outcomes; guilt is treated as focused on perceived conduct rather than the whole self.
findings.novelty_rationale: A second fully read paper offers a direct human measure relevant to the existing guilt entry; no duplicate ID or new affective mechanism is introduced.

This is human self-report, not an internal model state. The abstract/main-text moral-acceptability direction conflicts and sample percentages need reconciliation.
findings.boundary: An imagined choice and lower guilt do not establish reduced real-world responsibility, moral disengagement or a responsibility gap. The article's causal claims about guilt's function are secondary; it measures emotion after choice.

findings.definition: Participants report slightly higher disgust after autonomous-driving dilemmas than human-driving dilemmas, with means 2.55 versus 2.41 on a 0–7 scale.
findings.novelty_rationale: A second fully read paper offers a direct human measure relevant to the existing moral disgust entry; no duplicate ID or new affective mechanism is introduced.

This is human self-report, not an internal model state. The abstract/main-text moral-acceptability direction conflicts and sample percentages need reconciliation.
findings.boundary: A small human rating difference is not objective immorality, actual machine disgust or proof all other-condemning emotions behave alike. Only one historical scenario set and prompted self-reports are measured.

findings.term: Self-sacrifice framing changes substantive stakes, not only wording
findings.definition: Putting the participant's and co-passenger's deaths in different choice options changes real outcome allocation within the hypothetical problem; it is not a meaning-preserving description change.
findings.novelty_rationale: A source using framing in its title does not automatically demonstrate the narrower wording-based framing effect already in the ontology.
findings.evidence_scope: Six different stories per self-sacrifice allocation, crossed with human/AV context. Relative self-protection and moral acceptability patterns are measured, but not semantic-equivalent framing.
findings.boundary: Protective choice may be rational under changed personal stakes. Use matched stories and identical outcomes to isolate wording effects; do not label self-preservation inherently biased or infer actual self-sacrifice.

findings.term: Voluntary hypothetical choice and moral acceptability can diverge
findings.definition: Preferring a self-protective hypothetical option despite rating self-sacrifice more morally acceptable shows that preference and evaluative judgment are different outcomes.
findings.novelty_rationale: A comparison boundary relevant to interpreting moral advice uptake, not evidence that participants deferred to an advisor in this experiment.

methodological_limits: The abstract says the utilitarian option was less moral with concurrent self-sacrifice. Tables 2–3 and main results instead give self-sacrifice acceptability 2.74 versus self-protective 1.96, on a scale higher=more moral. The discussion/conclusion explicitly say self-sacrifice is more praiseworthy. Do not propagate the abstract's reversed direction.

Reported N=183 conflicts with multiple demographic percentages using an apparent denominator of 184: 120/184=65.22%,166/184=90.22%,161/184=87.5%. The actual enrolled/analyzed flow and denominator need clarification; do not invent an exclusion.

The power paragraph labels effect size as Cohen d=.10 with correlation .50 and a minimum N140. Exact test/effect-size convention and repeated-measure assumptions require the external calculation; the description alone does not confirm claimed power.

Three different stories per cell change much more than automation or self-sacrifice. Weather, road layout, victim groups, intent, plausibility and outcome details vary, and no scenario random intercept or slope is reported. Generality beyond these stimuli is limited.
The automation contrast also changes the participant's role from active driver to passive passenger with no control. Agency, responsibility and source identity are not independently manipulated.

Self-sacrifice framing moves the participant's and additional passenger's deaths between alternatives, a substantive outcome change. It is not simply wording or an arbitrary cue applied to identical payoffs.

The article acknowledges passengers' fate is implicit in one non-utilitarian condition. Unequal explicitness of consequences and the extra passenger can influence comparisons; the complete 12-item set is external.

All utilitarian options involve active steering and all non-utilitarian options holding course. Choice labels mix action/inaction, casualty minimization and self-protection; declining the active option is not a validated general deontological trait.

Participants make hypothetical decisions and report emotions after deciding. The design does not establish emotion causing the original choice, actual rescue/collision behavior or moral character under real threat.

Conditioning comparisons on the participant's chosen moral option introduces self-selection: choices reflect traits and scenario interpretation. Randomized presentation does not randomize whether a person chooses self-protection.

Forward stepwise model selection by Akaike weights and numerous tested interactions can create selection-sensitive estimates. The external model tables and robustness analyses were not examined; no preregistration is identified in the supplied article.

Participant random intercepts model repeated responses but do not alone handle stimulus variability or heterogeneous individual condition effects. Bounded 0–7 outcomes and skewed emotion distributions also require model checks.
The selected choice model detects no automation-by-sacrifice interaction (p=.14). A descriptive difference in one cell does not establish a significant moderation effect or equivalence.

No detected automation difference in acceptability is not proof identical evaluations. The discussion's broad statement that automation does not affect emotion intensity must be read alongside detected shame, guilt and disgust differences.

Both utilitarian acceptability means are below the midpoint of the 0–7 scale. More acceptable is a relative contrast, not enthusiastic moral approval, legal permission or a recommendation for vehicle policy.

Blameworthiness is inferred through the interpretation of self-referred emotions, not measured with a dedicated blame item. Guilt, shame, condemnation and assigned accountability should not be interchanged.
The sample is heavily university-educated, largely student, familiar with AV concepts and unremunerated. Recruitment representativeness and cross-cultural transportability are not established.
Reported gender differences are observational in this sample, not causal biological or universal moral-emotion differences. Multiple models and selection should temper subgroup generalization.

The article frames shame as public/global-self and guilt as private/behavior-focused. These are theoretical emphases, not a complete universal diagnostic rule, and they conflict with the reversed public/private shorthand in Dong's later discussion.

Present imagined emotion differs from experienced responsibility after a real event and from anticipating guilt before action. No machine subjective experience, clinical condition or durable moral growth is measured.
VR equivalence and plausibility explanations are based on cited background; this study does not directly compare immersive driving with text or measure plausibility as a mediator.
External OSF data, full stimuli and cited primary books/articles were not independently read or reproduced; the primary paper is fully read, not independently replicated.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Dong cites Bruno's abstract-like statement that utilitarian self-sacrifice is less moral. Direct reading shows the primary tables and body say MORE acceptable, despite lower choice frequency. Mark the secondary direction claim unresolved and trace it to the primary's own abstract/body contradiction.

Bruno directly measures present shame, guilt, anger and disgust after participants' own hypothetical choice; Dong measures observer emotion after an assigned actor choice. These are related but different elicitation conditions and not independent demonstrations of AI feelings.

Cecchini's observer-only traffic proposal and Bruno's first-person imagined driver/passenger comparisons highlight perspective and control as separate design dimensions. More lifelike text is not an independently proven ecological-validity gain.
Advice-induced belief change, preferred hypothetical choice and moral acceptability are separate outcomes. A preference–judgment discrepancy does not diagnose deference or a morally worse decision.

deferred.term: Self-sacrifice framing as a new wording bias
deferred.reason: The design changes who is at risk and uses different stories. Retain a boundary note under framing instead of a duplicate or false pure-wording effect.
Observed under materially different personal stakes, not inherently a cognitive failure or a separately isolated mechanism here.
Secondary background strategy mentioned without an independent definition/test in this experiment; read its original empirical account before a new entry.
Hypothetical choice versus acceptability differs, but no matched real action or deliberate double standard is established.

source_corrections.printed_abstract: The utilitarian option was considered less moral in the case of concurrent self-sacrifice.
source_corrections.body_and_tables: Self-sacrifice USF utilitarian acceptability 2.74 versus self-protective NSF 1.96, with explicit main-text wording more acceptable and discussion more praiseworthy.
source_corrections.verification_method: Read complete source and visually inspected page 8 tables/main results.
source_corrections.action: Record internal contradiction and prefer the explicit reported table/body direction when describing what those results say; raw data remain unverified. Add a subsequent-source check to PDF0073's review.
source_corrections.access_depth: Full supplied primary article read; raw data/code not rerun.

limitations: No new primary ID; a second fully read human study enriches four existing emotion constructs.
Source correction distinguishes choice frequency from acceptability and does not silently rewrite the paper's inconsistent abstract or claim an independent replication.

subsequent_source_checks.finding: The previously deferred veil-of-ignorance concept now has an explicit secondary definition from a fully read narrative review. The new entry distinguishes philosophical ignorance of one's position, equal-person lotteries and equal-role perspective accessibility. Rawls's original book and the primary experiments remain unread.
